facts: Notebook (feed): The Oaks are 8-1 after an 0-9 start through rookie camp and the preseason. Was the 0-9 really about rest and experiments, as Elliot Abraham said in C111, or did the team change something, and will Abraham say so now that it is working? Has the Draymond Green situation settled for him? Is this a defensive team now, or does Wilson Shepard's offense still have another gear? How much of Mike Paulson's attention does the A's offseason take from the Oaks? And with Jerami Grant's failed medical still with the league, what does the roster look like when the hard part of the schedule arrives?
Oaks — season-state (early-season), C116: Was the 0-9 start by design, and is this a defensive team now?

Notebook (feed): Ten games into their first season, the Oakland Oaks are the number one team in the NBA.com power rankings, ranked first of all 31 teams, and holding the top spot from the week before. The rankings are built on season record and recent form, and the Oaks had both: 9-1 when they came out, 3-0 over the last week, 6-1 over the last two weeks. They earned it against real opponents. Four of the teams in the top nine are teams the Oaks have already beaten: Detroit, ranked 3rd, beaten 91-78 on the road; Oklahoma City, ranked 4th, beaten 101-95 in the Cup opener at home; New York, ranked 6th, beaten 115-93 on the road; and Philadelphia, ranked 8th, beaten 120-106 on the road after trailing by two going into the fourth. Ranked 2nd was San Antonio. The rankings only update once a week, and these came out a game behind. Since then the Spurs came into Oakland for a Cup game and won 126-117, handing the Oaks their first ever home loss. So number one is now 9-2, number two is 8-2, and the gap at the top is half a game. For an expansion team that went 0-9 through rookie camp and the preseason, with a first-year head coach and a first-time GM, being ranked first in the league at all is the story.
Oaks — team-update (early-season), C116: Number one in the NBA in year one: the Oaks top the power rankings, a game before the Spurs came to town

Notebook (feed): The Spurs handed the Oaks their first ever home loss. San Antonio came into Oakland for a Cup game in front of a 99 percent crowd and left with a 126-117 win, only the Oaks' second loss of the season. It was even for three quarters. The Oaks trailed by 8 after a slow 20-point first, won the second 35-25 to lead 55-53 at the half, and it was tied 90-90 going into the fourth. Then the offense that shot 80 percent in Denver went cold. The Oaks scored 27 in the fourth, lost the quarter by 9, and finished 41 of 95 from the field, 43 percent, and 12 of 36 from three. They also left points at the line, 23 of 32, and turned it over 14 times after just 5 in Denver. T. Jerome was the exception again. Off the bench he scored 23 in 21 minutes, all six of his field goals from three on 6 of 8, plus 5 of 7 at the line and 2 steals. That is 19, 28 and 23 in his last three games, and the case for a bigger role is getting hard to ignore. Outside of Jerome the Oaks were 6 of 28 from three. AJ Dybantsa led the starters with 19 on 6 of 14, 3 of 5 from deep, and 4 of 5 at the line. Wendell Carter Jr. had a 14-point, 12-rebound double-double with 4 offensive boards but went 6 of 11 at the line. Adash Stanley had 14, 5 rebounds and 7 assists, and Austin Reaves had 13, 6 rebounds and 6 assists with 4 turnovers. Dillon Brooks scored 13 but needed 19 shots, 5 of 19 and 0 of 6 from three. Harry Hayward came back to earth after his perfect night in Denver, 2 of 9 and 1 of 6 from three, but grabbed 10 rebounds and added 3 assists in 20 minutes. T. Henderson Jr. got back on the floor and went 2 for 2 in 12 minutes. B. Simmons was a DNP for the sixth straight game, with B. James Jr., J. Tate and Coen Carr also sitting. The five-game win streak is over. The Oaks fall to 9-2 and 2-1 in Cup play, and are now scoring 113.9 a game and allowing 95.1.
Oaks — game-result (early-season), C116: The Spurs hand the Oaks their first home loss. Spurs 126 - Oaks 117

Notebook (feed): One cycle after this page asked whether Wilson Shepard's offense still had another gear, the Oaks found it in Denver. They won their second NBA Cup game 147-114, the most points in franchise history, topping the 135 they put up in Toronto. Oakland led by 5 after one, by 18 at the half and by 23 after three, then scored 42 in the fourth. The shooting numbers barely look real: 63 of 79 from the field, 80 percent, and 19 of 26 from three, 73 percent. The Oaks handed out 40 assists against just 5 turnovers, scored 72 in the paint and 12 on the break, and their bench outscored most starting fives with 56. Five Oaks did not miss a shot. AJ Dybantsa went 8 for 8 for 18, Wendell Carter Jr. went 8 for 8 for 17 with 9 rebounds, Adash Stanley went 6 for 6 for 15 with 3 of 3 from deep, Harry Hayward went 5 for 5 and 4 for 4 from three for 14, and J. Valanciunas went 3 for 3 for 6 with 6 rebounds in 10 minutes. That is 30 for 30 between them. The leading scorer came off the bench. T. Jerome scored 28 on 12 of 16 with 10 assists in 28 minutes, his second big night as the sixth man after his 19, 7 and 7 in Toronto. Austin Reaves bounced back from his 4 of 14 night in Philadelphia with 27 points on 11 of 14, a perfect 5 of 5 from three, 12 assists and 2 steals in a team-high 41 minutes. Dillon Brooks added 14. Hayward keeps forcing the issue. In 19 minutes he added 4 assists to his perfect shooting, and he is now 9 of 10 from three over his last six games. G. Trent Jr. hit 2 threes in 3 minutes and J. Champagnie handed out 4 assists. B. Simmons was a DNP for the fifth straight game, and T. Henderson Jr., B. James Jr., J. Tate and Coen Carr also sat. The Oaks win their fifth straight, move to 9-1 and 2-0 in Cup play, and are now scoring 113.6 a game while allowing 92.0.

Notebook (feed): Ten cycles ago this page was asking Wilson Shepard for answers. The Oaks went 0-4 in rookie camp and 0-5 in the preseason, 0-9 before they had played a game that counted, and in C109 the media wanted to know why the team was losing and why the full roster had never been on the floor together. Shepard, a first-year head coach who spent the previous season as an offensive assistant in Minnesota, kept saying the same thing. In C107 he said the Oaks would "catch people off guard this year." In C109 he said, "We're still finding our rhythm. The guys are putting in the work, and I'm confident we'll tighten up and be ready for the real deal. We're not getting the results we want, but we're not letting it get us down either." In C110, after the loss to Miami, he said the full team had yet to suit up as one, that opening night would show a team nobody had seen, and that he was not worried. The fans were. Nine games into the real deal, the Oaks are 8-1, have won four straight and are 1-0 in the NBA Cup. They beat Charlotte 85-82 in the franchise's first game, coming back from 11 down after three, won in Detroit, New York and Washington, lost by four in Indiana after coming back from 20 down, then routed Toronto 135-75 and beat Oklahoma City, Orlando and Philadelphia. They are scoring 109.9 a game and allowing 89.6, a margin of more than 20 points a night. The surprise is how they are winning. Shepard came in as the offensive specialist, but the early identity is defense: Charlotte scored 82, Detroit 78, Toronto 75 and Washington 62. He has also found rotation pieces nobody expected, like second-round rookie Harry Hayward, and kept the bench fresh, with nobody playing more than 28 minutes in the Toronto rout. After the opener he laughed that his ears were still ringing, then said the next loss could be a game away and the job was to build on the good and eliminate the bad. The other half of this story is the man above him. Mike Paulson is president of operations for an 8-1 expansion team, with Elliot Abraham running the day-to-day as GM, and he is also the GM of the A's in the middle of an offseason that has already seen Vinnie Keane retire, Carmen Mesa traded to the Phillies, Mark Aitken drawing Angels interest in free agency and Benji Dillon undecided. In C110 fans worried that a first-year coach, a first-time GM and a front office chief busy with a World Series run was too much uncertainty. So far the Oaks have answered that. Then there is Elliot Abraham, the first-time GM who has said almost nothing since C111. That cycle, with the team 0-9, he told the media nobody was panicking, that the losing was intentional and that every variation they tried was data for the long term. He also said the Draymond Green trade "wasn't ideal form" for a player the community reveres, and that Jerami Grant's status was a matter the league was looking into. In C112 Elias Varek confirmed Grant had failed his medical and credited Paulson and Abraham with building a quality team in one offseason. Abraham has not spoken since. His path here is not a typical basketball one: born in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, adopted young by an American family, MIT, the man who built the first successful professional pickleball league, then senior operations under Varek at Civis Systems and Paulson's day-to-day operator in his one season with the Chicago Bulls before Oakland hired him in C101. The Bulls beat his Oaks in the preseason in C110. He lives in Jack London, has been seen staying late in the clubhouse after wins, and around the waterfront he is still more of a familiar face than a public one.

The shooting numbers barely look real: 63 of 79 from the field, 80 percent, and 19 of 26 from three, 73 percent. The Oaks handed out 40 assists against just 5 turnovers, scored 72 in the paint and 12 on the break, and their bench outscored most starting fives with 56. Five Oaks did not miss a shot. AJ Dybantsa went 8 for 8 for 18, Wendell Carter Jr. went 8 for 8 for 17 with 9 rebounds, Adash Stanley went 6 for 6 for 15 with 3 of 3 from deep, Harry Hayward went 5 for 5 and 4 for 4 from three for 14, and J. Valanciunas went 3 for 3 for 6 with 6 rebounds in 10 minutes. That is 30 for 30 between them. The leading scorer came off the bench. T. Jerome scored 28 on 12 of 16 with 10 assists in 28 minutes, his second big night as the sixth man after his 19, 7 and 7 in Toronto. Austin Reaves bounced back from his 4 of 14 night in Philadelphia with 27 points on 11 of 14, a perfect 5 of 5 from three, 12 assists and 2 steals in a team-high 41 minutes. Dillon Brooks added 14. Hayward keeps forcing the issue. In 19 minutes he added 4 assists to his perfect shooting, and he is now 9 of 10 from three over his last six games. G. Trent Jr. hit 2 threes in 3 minutes and J. Champagnie handed out 4 assists. B. Simmons was a DNP for the fifth straight game, and T. Henderson Jr., B. James Jr., J. Tate and Coen Carr also sat. The Oaks win their fifth straight, move to 9-1 and 2-0 in Cup play, and are now scoring 113.6 a game while allowing 92.0.

Notebook (feed): Ten cycles ago this page was asking Wilson Shepard for answers. The Oaks went 0-4 in rookie camp and 0-5 in the preseason, 0-9 before they had played a game that counted, and in C109 the media wanted to know why the team was losing and why the full roster had never been on the floor together. Shepard, a first-year head coach who spent the previous season as an offensive assistant in Minnesota, kept saying the same thing. In C107 he said the Oaks would "catch people off guard this year." In C109 he said, "We're still finding our rhythm. The guys are putting in the work, and I'm confident we'll tighten up and be ready for the real deal. We're not getting the results we want, but we're not letting it get us down either." In C110, after the loss to Miami, he said the full team had yet to suit up as one, that opening night would show a team nobody had seen, and that he was not worried. The fans were. Nine games into the real deal, the Oaks are 8-1, have won four straight and are 1-0 in the NBA Cup. They beat Charlotte 85-82 in the franchise's first game, coming back from 11 down after three, won in Detroit, New York and Washington, lost by four in Indiana after coming back from 20 down, then routed Toronto 135-75 and beat Oklahoma City, Orlando and Philadelphia. They are scoring 109.9 a game and allowing 89.6, a margin of more than 20 points a night. The surprise is how they are winning. Shepard came in as the offensive specialist, but the early identity is defense: Charlotte scored 82, Detroit 78, Toronto 75 and Washington 62. He has also found rotation pieces nobody expected, like second-round rookie Harry Hayward, and kept the bench fresh, with nobody playing more than 28 minutes in the Toronto rout. After the opener he laughed that his ears were still ringing, then said the next loss could be a game away and the job was to build on the good and eliminate the bad. The other half of this story is the man above him. Mike Paulson is president of operations for an 8-1 expansion team, with Elliot Abraham running the day-to-day as GM, and he is also the GM of the A's in the middle of an offseason that has already seen Vinnie Keane retire, Carmen Mesa traded to the Phillies, Mark Aitken drawing Angels interest in free agency and Benji Dillon undecided. In C110 fans worried that a first-year coach, a first-time GM and a front office chief busy with a World Series run was too much uncertainty. So far the Oaks have answered that. Then there is Elliot Abraham, the first-time GM who has said almost nothing since C111. That cycle, with the team 0-9, he told the media nobody was panicking, that the losing was intentional and that every variation they tried was data for the long term. He also said the Draymond Green trade "wasn't ideal form" for a player the community reveres, and that Jerami Grant's status was a matter the league was looking into. In C112 Elias Varek confirmed Grant had failed his medical and credited Paulson and Abraham with building a quality team in one offseason. Abraham has not spoken since. His path here is not a typical basketball one: born in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, adopted young by an American family, MIT, the man who built the first successful professional pickleball league, then senior operations under Varek at Civis Systems and Paulson's day-to-day operator in his one season with the Chicago Bulls before Oakland hired him in C101. The Bulls beat his Oaks in the preseason in C110. He lives in Jack London, has been seen staying late in the clubhouse after wins, and around the waterfront he is still more of a familiar face than a public one.

angleRead.text: I'm heading to the Oaks game tonight to get a feel for the crowd and the mood in the room. The team is 8-1 after a rough preseason, and I want to see how they're being received by the fans in West Oakland. I've heard that the A's offseason is taking some attention away from the Oaks, so I'll be looking for reactions to that. I'll also be talking to some of the regulars at the stadium to get their take on the team's performance so far.
